1.title: Solution Design, Workflow Integration and Stakeholder Communication
1.text: Welcome to Module ten: Solution Design, Workflow Integration and Stakeholder Communication. This module covers solution design, workflow integration and stakeholder communication. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. How Claude supports design, build and iteration of a solution. How to fit Claude into an existing workflow: augment a step or redesign the flow. Patterns that work: draft and review, triage, extract, summarize. When to escalate to Developers or Architects. How to communicate value and limits honestly to stakeholders.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Onboarding Kit
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Onboarding Kit. H R wants a new-hire onboarding kit: checklist, welcome email series, an F A Q and a short interactive quiz. The H R lead uses Claude to draft the structure, build an artifact quiz, test it with sample answers, and revise after feedback from two managers.

1.title: Supporting Solution Design and Iteration
1.text: Supporting Solution Design and Iteration. Design. How Claude helps: Options with trade-offs, outlines, mock-ups, process diagrams, templates. Your role: Choose, adapt to your context. Build. How Claude helps: Draft documents, forms, spreadsheets with formulas, slide decks, simple interactive artifacts. Your role: Review, test, own the result. Test. How Claude helps: Sample inputs, edge cases, checklists, "what could go wrong" lists. Your role: Run the tests; judge the outcomes. Iterate. How Claude helps: Revise from feedback; compare versions; track changes in a summary. Your role: Collect real user feedback. Document. How Claude helps: Instructions, F A Q s, handover notes. Your role: Confirm accuracy. Prototype fast, validate with users. A quick artifact or draft is a conversation starter, not a finished product.

1.title: Supporting Solution Design and Iteration, continued
1.text: Supporting Solution Design and Iteration, continued. Small, simple solutions (templates, checklists, spreadsheets, Projects, simple artifacts) are the Associate's territory. For anything that needs code in production, A P I (application programming interface) calls, databases or system integration, escalate (section four).

1.title: Fitting Claude into a Workflow
1.text: Fitting Claude into a Workflow. The figure shows this: Augment a step to speed up one task inside the current process, or redesign the process around what Claude does well.

1.title: Fitting Claude into a Workflow, continued
1.text: Fitting Claude into a Workflow, continued. Augment. What changes: One step gets faster or better; the process stays. Example: Agents get draft replies from Claude and send after review. Risk: Low. Redesign. What changes: Steps are removed, merged or reordered. Example: Instead of five hand-offs, Claude triages and drafts, a person approves once. Risk: Higher: needs a pilot and clear ownership. Workflow patterns that work.

1.title: Fitting Claude into a Workflow, continued
1.text: Fitting Claude into a Workflow, continued. Draft and review. Claude drafts; a person edits and approves. Triage and route. Claude classifies and tags; a person handles the exceptions. Extract and structure. Claude pulls fields from documents; a person spot-checks. Summarize and decide. Claude summarizes long inputs; a person decides. Research and brief. Claude gathers and cites; a person verifies and concludes. Building blocks inside Claude: Projects (standing instructions and knowledge), Skills (repeatable methods), connectors (Google Drive, Gmail, Slack and others), artifacts (shareable outputs), memory (continuity) (Modules eleven and twelve). Make it stick.

1.title: Fitting Claude into a Workflow, continued
1.text: Fitting Claude into a Workflow, continued. Name an owner for the prompt, the Project and the quality of the results. Write down when to use Claude and when not to. Keep review steps where errors matter. Share the prompts and Projects so everyone gets consistent results. Train the team (examples, do's and don'ts, how to verify). Track K P I s (time saved, error rate, satisfaction) and review them. Exam tip: The safe answer for integration: start with augmentation and a human review, pilot, measure, then redesign where evidence supports it.

1.title: Know the Boundary: When to Escalate
1.text: Know the Boundary: When to Escalate. The figure shows this: The Associate builds with the product's own features and escalates A P I, agent and architecture work to Developers and Architects.

1.title: Know the Boundary: When to Escalate, continued
1.text: Know the Boundary: When to Escalate, continued. Prompts, Projects, instructions, knowledge. Building against the A P I, code that calls Claude. Skills, artifacts, connectors from the directory. Agents, automated multi-step pipelines, scheduled jobs at scale. Reviewing outputs and workflows. Integrations with core systems and databases. Pilots and measures. Security architecture, access control, data-residency design. Policy-compliant daily use. Enterprise-scale deployment design and evaluation frameworks. The exam guide says plainly that Associates recognize limitations and escalate more complex or technical work. Escalate when the solution needs custom code, automation without a human, large data volumes, or security and compliance design.

1.title: Know the Boundary: When to Escalate, continued
1.text: Know the Boundary: When to Escalate, continued. Bring a clear brief: the business goal, the current process, the data involved, volumes, risks and success measures.

1.title: Communicating Value and Limits
1.text: Communicating Value and Limits. Stakeholders need an honest picture: neither hype nor fear.

1.title: Communicating Value and Limits, continued
1.text: Communicating Value and Limits, continued. The figure shows this: Communicate value with evidence and limits with plain words: use a pilot result to support both.

1.title: Communicating Value and Limits, continued
1.text: Communicating Value and Limits, continued. Time saved on drafting, summarizing, analysis (use pilot numbers). Claude can be wrong or invent details; outputs are reviewed. Consistency of tone and format with Projects and Skills. It has a knowledge cutoff and only the tools and data you connect. Faster first drafts, so people spend time on judgment. Sensitive data rules apply; not every task is allowed. Scale: handles volume spikes. Bias can appear; people decisions need human oversight. Learning curve is short for common tasks. Usage limits and costs exist; effort and model choices matter.

1.title: Communicating Value and Limits, continued
1.text: Communicating Value and Limits, continued. Tailor the message: executives want outcomes, risk and cost; managers want workload and quality; staff want how it changes their job and what stays human; compliance wants data handling and review. Back claims with evidence from a pilot, not vendor promises: "In the pilot, reply drafting time fell from six to two minutes; four percent of drafts needed corrections of facts.". Never promise that Claude is always accurate, replaces staff review, or can do things it is not connected to do. Be open about what is still unknown and how you will learn it.

2.title: Communicating Value and Limits, continued
2.text: Communicating Value and Limits, continued. Show how people stay accountable: who reviews, who approves, who owns the policy. Exam tip: The best stakeholder message is balanced, evidence-based and specific: real benefits, real limits, a review plan and a next step. Exam tip: Pilot, measure, then scale: evidence from a small trial beats a promise, and any step Claude cannot do alone is a job for a Developer.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Design and iterate: Claude drafts options, prototypes, tests; you validate with users. Augment versus redesign: Augment a step (low risk), redesign the flow (pilot first). Patterns: Draft and review, triage and route, extract and structure, summarize and decide, research and brief. Make it stick: Owner, when-to-use rules, reviews, shared Projects, training, K P I s. Escalate: A P I integration, agents, automation at scale, systems integration, security architecture. Brief: Goal, process, data, volumes, risks, measures. Message: Evidence-based value plus plain limits plus review plan plus next step. Never promise: Perfect accuracy; replacing review; connections that do not exist.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Customer care agents currently write every reply from scratch. What is the lowest-risk way to bring Claude into this workflow? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Augmenting with a draft-and-review step is low risk and quick to pilot.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A manager wants Claude connected directly to the order database through custom code, with scheduled automatic updates. What should the Associate do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A P I integration and automation at scale belong to Developers and Architects.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Which message to the leadership team is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Specific evidence plus an honest limit and a control.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. What is the main difference between augmenting and redesigning a workflow? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Augmentation keeps the process; redesign reshapes it and needs more care.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. An H R lead builds a quiz artifact with Claude. What is the right next step? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A prototype is a conversation starter, so it is tested with sample answers and real users and revised before wider use.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Select two. Which two are good practices when rolling Claude into a team workflow? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and E. Naming an owner and keeping review steps where errors matter keep quality accountable as more people start using Claude.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Which statement about talking to compliance stakeholders is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Compliance wants to know what data enters Claude, which policy applies and who reviews outputs, not a promise of perfection.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Which workflow is a good "triage and route" example? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Classification with human exception handling is a safe and valuable pattern.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. A team cannot tell whether Claude helps. What should they do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Only measured evidence from a pilot compared with a baseline can show whether Claude actually helps, rather than opinions or guesses.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Which request should an Associate escalate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Secure integration across several internal systems with access controls is architecture work for a Developer or Architect, not an Associate task.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. What belongs in a good brief when escalating to a Developer? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A clear brief lets the technical team design the right solution.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all eleven answers. Question one: C. Question two: B. Question three: B. Question four: B. Question five: A. Question six: A and E. Question seven: B. Question eight: A. Question nine: A. Question ten: B. Question eleven: D. In the next module, we continue the course.
